cultivar: Roasted dried maize kernels; corn silk tea uses the dried, roasted silk threads from the cob
processing: Dried corn kernels are roasted until deep golden-brown with toasted spots, sometimes cracked, and packed whole or in large infusion bags; for corn silk tea the silk is dried and lightly roasted. Both are often blended with roasted barley.
harvest_season: Corn is harvested in late summer (August to September), dried and roasted through the year; the tea is served hot in winter and chilled in summer.
appearance_dry: Whole roasted kernels, golden-brown with dark toasted patches; corn silk tea is a tangle of pale tan threads.
appearance_liquor: Clear pale gold to light amber.
appearance_wet: Swollen, soft kernels that smell of popcorn; the silk turns into limp pale strands.
taste_profile: Sweet, soft and toasty, like popcorn or roasted sweetcorn, with no bitterness at all; corn silk tea is lighter, grassier and only faintly sweet.

brewing.notes: Simmer 20–30 g of roasted kernels in a litre of water for 10–15 minutes, or steep one large bag in boiling water for 10 minutes; chill for summer. Mixed half and half with barley tea it is the standard Korean table drink.

vintage_note: No vintage: a roasted grain sold year-round in one-litre tea bags, as whole roasted kernels, and bottled, with a best-before of around a year. The label distinguishes kernel tea (oksusu-cha) from corn silk tea (oksusu-suyeom-cha), which is the one sold in bottles as a light diet drink, and many packs are barley-and-corn blends. Roasting date is not stated, so buy from a Korean grocery with turnover.
description:
Corn tea is the sweet, popcorn-scented cousin of barley tea and one of the standard free drinks on a Korean restaurant table, poured warm from a kettle in winter and cold from a jug in summer. It comes from Gangwon province in the mountainous northeast, where corn is a staple crop, and it is the kind of drink nobody thinks about and everybody drinks.

The kernels are dried and roasted until they are golden-brown and toasty, and that roast is the entire flavour: a long, slow roast gives a sweet, rounded cup, a quick dark one gives something more bitter. A second product, corn silk tea, uses the fine threads from inside the husk, dried and lightly roasted, and gives a paler, grassier drink that is sold in bottles everywhere in Korea.

Brewed properly, which means simmered for a while rather than steeped like a tea bag, it is soft, sweet and slightly nutty with no bitterness or astringency, and it is probably the most child-friendly hot drink there is. Most households mix it with roasted barley, which adds body and a slight bitterness that keeps the sweetness in check.

It is sold as whole roasted kernels, as big infusion bags, and bottled; there is no vintage to think about, only freshness, since roasted corn goes stale within a year. Check whether a pack is kernel tea, corn silk tea or a barley blend, because they taste quite different.

Corn silk tea has traditionally been drunk as a light, diuretic everyday drink; the kernel tea is simply comfort in a cup. Try it alongside barley tea and buckwheat tea to see how three roasted grains give three different drinks.
